chunks: Ali, from his father, from Ismail ibn Marar, from Yunus and Ibn Abi Umeyr, both together, from Abu Ayyub al-Khazzaz, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, who said:

Two boys were born to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) at the same time, so he ordered Zayd ibn Ali to buy for him two camels for the Aqeeqa. It was a time of high prices, so he bought one for him, but the second was difficult for him. So he said to Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), 'The second has become difficult for me, so give its price in charity.' He (peace be upon him) said, 'No, seek it until you are able to afford it, for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, loves the pouring out of blood (of sacrifice) and the feeding of food.'

key_terms.إِطْعَامَ الطَّعَامِ: Feeding of food (referring to distributing the meat)
key_terms.إِهْرَاقَ الدِّمَاءِ: Pouring out of blood (referring to the act of slaughter/sacrifice)
key_terms.عَقِيقَة: Aqeeqa: Sacrificial animal offered for a newborn child

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on Aqeeqa if one cannot afford two animals?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Kafi highlights the preference for the actual physical sacrifice (Aqeeqa) over its monetary equivalent (Qimah), even during periods of high inflation, underscoring the ritual's tangible nature. Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) emphasizes that Allah loves the act of 'pouring blood' and 'feeding food,' linking the ritual directly to the Prophet Muhammad's tradition and the spiritual merit of providing sustenance. This ruling reinforces the Shia scholarly view that while financial ease is considered, the primary obligation remains the offering of the animal itself rather than its cash value.
